questions.question: A round pizza is cut into 8 equal slices. Every straight cut runs from the centre point of the pizza out to the edge, and each of those cuts measures 6 cm. What is the correct name for one of these 6 cm cuts?
options: The radius of the pizza
The circumference of the pizza
The diameter of the pizza
Pi (π) of the pizza
questions.explain: A straight line from the centre of a circle out to the edge is the radius. The common trap is calling it the diameter — the diameter goes all the way across through the centre, so on this pizza it would be 12 cm, not 6 cm.

questions.question: A round bannock is cut into 8 equal slices. Two cuts that sit opposite each other line up to make one straight line that starts at the edge, passes through the centre, and ends at the edge on the other side. That straight line measures 12 cm. Which statement names this 12 cm line correctly?
options: It is the radius, because it is made of straight cuts of the circle
It is the diameter, because it goes right through the centre from one edge to the other
It is the circumference, because it is the longest measurement of the circle
It is pi (π), because it is the number that describes the middle of a circle
questions.explain: Edge to edge through the centre is the diameter, and it is always double the radius (here 12 cm across, 6 cm from centre to edge). The usual mix-up is calling this line the radius — the radius is only half of it.

questions.question: A circular cookie is cut into 4 equal quarters. The curved outside edge of each quarter measures 9 cm, and all four quarters have the same curved edge. If you add the four curved edges together, which measurement of the circle have you found?
options: The diameter, the distance straight across the circle through the centre
The radius, the distance from the centre out to the edge
The circumference, the distance all the way around the outside of the circle
Pi (π), the number you get by measuring straight across the circle
questions.explain: The circumference is the distance all the way around the outside, so the four curved edges joined together (9 + 9 + 9 + 9 = 36 cm) make the circumference. A common trap is picking the straight-across measurement — that one is the diameter, and it is a straight line, not a curve.

questions.question: A circle is drawn like a pizza with 6 equal slices. Each straight cut goes from the centre point out to the edge, and each cut measures 7 cm. You want to draw this same circle with a compass. How far apart should the compass point and pencil be set?
options: 14 cm, because the compass must reach right across the whole circle
3.5 cm, because the compass opening is half of one cut
42 cm, because there are 6 cuts of 7 cm each
7 cm, because the compass opening is the radius, from the centre to the edge
questions.explain: A compass draws by keeping the point at the centre, so its opening is the radius — here 7 cm. The classic mistake is opening it to 14 cm, which is the diameter and would draw a circle twice as wide as the one described.

questions.question: A circle has a diameter d = 18 cm. Which statement about this circle is true?
options: r = 9 cm, because the radius is half the diameter
r = 18 cm, because the radius and the diameter are the same line
r = 36 cm, because the radius is double the diameter
r = 18 ÷ π, because the radius is found by dividing by pi
questions.explain: The diameter is always two radii long, so r = d ÷ 2 = 18 ÷ 2 = 9 cm. The trap is doubling instead of halving — doubling turns a radius into a diameter, not the other way around.

questions.question: Manjot is drawing a circle for a science poster at his school in Kelowna. The circle must have a diameter of 12 cm. He has a ruler and a compass. Which setting should he use?
options: Open the compass to 12 cm, because that is the number given
Open the compass to 6 cm, because the compass opening is the radius
Open the compass to 24 cm, because he needs to reach both edges
Open the compass to about 3.8 cm, because 12 ÷ π gives the setting
questions.explain: The compass opening is the distance from the centre to the edge, which is the radius, so use 12 ÷ 2 = 6 cm. Setting it to 12 cm is the most common slip — that would draw a circle 24 cm across.

questions.question: In every circle, no matter how big or small, the circumference is always a little more than 3 times one particular measurement. Which measurement is it?
options: Half of the radius
The radius — the circumference is about 3.14 radii long
The diameter — the circumference is about 3.14 diameters long
The diameter multiplied by itself
questions.explain: Pi (π ≈ 3.14) is how many times the diameter fits around the circle, so C is about 3.14 × d. The frequent error is using the radius instead — the circumference is a bit more than 6 radii, not 3.

questions.question: A circle has a radius r = 5 cm. Which expression shows the circumference of this circle?
questions.explain: Circumference is π times the diameter, and the diameter here is 2 × 5 = 10 cm, so the expression is 2 × π × 5. The one that says π × 5 is the classic trap: it uses the radius where the diameter belongs, giving only half the true circumference.

questions.question: A round trampoline in a Surrey backyard is advertised as 3.6 m across at its widest point. The safety net for it is sold by radius size. Which net does the family need?
options: A net for a radius of 1.8 m
A net for a radius of 3.6 m
A net for a radius of 7.2 m
A net for a radius of about 1.1 m
questions.explain: Across at the widest point means the diameter, so the radius is 3.6 ÷ 2 = 1.8 m. The most common mistake is ordering 3.6 m as the radius, which would fit a trampoline twice as wide.

questions.question: Jayden has a circular garden stepping stone with a radius of 4 cm. He writes: C = π × 4, which is about 12.6 cm. His teacher says the answer is wrong. What is Jayden's mistake?
options: He should have used 3 instead of π to keep the numbers simple, so the answer should be 3 × 4 = 12 cm exactly
He put the radius where the formula needs the diameter, so he should use π × 8, which is about 25.1 cm
He should have added the radius twice at the end, so the answer should be 12.6 + 4 + 4, which is about 20.6 cm
He should have divided by π instead of multiplying, so the answer should be 4 ÷ π, which is about 1.3 cm
questions.explain: Circumference is π times the diameter, and the diameter is double the radius (4 × 2 = 8 cm), giving about 25.1 cm. Using π × radius is the single most common circle error and always gives exactly half the real circumference.

questions.question: Ravi is painting the biggest possible circle on a square wooden tile for a school art project. The tile measures 24 cm along each side, and the circle must just touch all four sides. How should he set his compass to draw the circle?
options: Open the compass to 24 cm
Open the compass to 48 cm
Open the compass to 12 cm
Open the compass to 6 cm
questions.explain: The circle touching all four sides is 24 cm at its widest, so 24 cm is the diameter and the compass opening (the radius) is 24 ÷ 2 = 12 cm. Setting the compass to 24 cm is the usual trap — that circle would be 48 cm across and run right off the tile.

questions.question: Ella measures her bike wheel and finds it is 35 cm from the centre hub straight out to the edge of the tire. The sticker on the bike frame calls it a 70 cm wheel. Are the sticker and Ella's measurement describing the same wheel?
options: No — the wheel should be labelled 35 × π, or about 110 cm, since a wheel's size is its circumference
No — a 70 cm wheel must be twice as big as the wheel Ella measured, because 70 is double 35
Yes — 70 cm must be the circumference, since a wheel sticker always gives the distance around the tire
Yes — Ella measured the radius, and 70 cm is the diameter, which is always double the radius
questions.explain: Centre to edge is the radius, and doubling it gives the diameter: 35 × 2 = 70 cm, so both describe the same wheel. The trap is treating the radius and diameter as two different-sized wheels instead of two ways of measuring one circle.
